lines: In 2005, one billion people were online.
Today, about five and a half billion are.
That is two-thirds of humanity. But the
last billion is the hardest. This is the
story of the global internet, told in
data. We will look at who is connected,
who is not, and what it will take to close
the gap, one connection at a time.
Start with the headline. Around 5.5
billion people used the internet in 2024.
That sounds like success, and in many ways
it is. In less than two decades, the
internet became the default infrastructure
of modern life. We use it to learn, work,
bank, vote, and stay in touch. But a
global average hides the story. If about
two-thirds are online, roughly one in
three people is still offline. That is
about 2.6 billion people. So the question
is not whether the internet matters. It is
who gets to use it.
The growth curve is one of the fastest
adoption stories in history. In 2005, just
over one billion people were online. By
2010, the number had passed two billion.
By 2015, it was over three billion. By
2020, the pandemic pushed millions more
online for school, work, and healthcare,
almost overnight. By 2024, the world
crossed five and a half billion. But look
closely at the shape of the curve. It is
slowing. The easy connections are already
made. The people still offline are harder
to reach: remote communities, low-income
households, and regions where
infrastructure is expensive to build.
Now let us break the average down by
region. In Europe, around 92 percent of
people are online. In the Americas, about
87 percent. In the Arab States, about 70
percent. In the Asia-Pacific region,
roughly two-thirds. In Africa, around 37
percent, which means most people there are
still offline. These gaps are not
accidents. They follow geography, income,
electricity, and policy. A country with
dense cities and strong fiber can connect
people quickly. A country with rural
populations and high construction costs
faces a longer, more expensive path. Every
new cable and every new tower changes who
can take part. The global map of the
internet is also a map of inequality.
For many people, the first connection is
not a laptop. It is a phone. Mobile
broadband has been the on-ramp to the
internet across low- and middle-income
countries. A single tower can reach a
village that fiber has not reached yet. A
prepaid SIM can be bought without a bank
account, and that changes everything for a
family that has never had a contract. That
is why mobile coverage has expanded faster
than fixed broadband. But coverage is not
the same as usage. You can have a signal
and still be offline, because you cannot
afford a smartphone, a data plan, or the
electricity to charge it.
Affordability is the quiet barrier. The UN
broadband target is that entry-level
broadband should cost no more than 2
percent of monthly income. In many
countries, it costs far more. For a family
living on a few dollars a day, one
gigabyte can take a significant share of
the budget, sometimes a whole day's
earnings. The result is a behavior we see
everywhere. People ration data. They watch
less video. They skip updates. They share
a phone. They wait for free Wi-Fi at the
market or the school. Being online is not
a simple yes or no. It is a spectrum of
how much you can afford to take part.
Speed is another divide. Median fixed
broadband speeds vary dramatically by
country and region. In some markets,
gigabit connections are common. In others,
a few megabits per second is normal. Speed
matters because modern services assume it.
Video calls, online classes, cloud tools,
and telehealth all need stable bandwidth.
A slow connection can turn a digital
opportunity into a frustrating delay, and
a student may miss the whole lesson while
the video buffers. Speed is also not only
about downloads. Upload speed decides
whether you can speak, teach, or sell to
the world. A farmer who cannot upload a
photo of a crop cannot ask for help or
find a buyer.
So who is still left out? The pattern is
consistent. Rural households are less
likely to be online than urban households.
Women are less likely than men in many
countries. Older people, people with
disabilities, and lower-income households
face additional barriers, from the cost of
a device to a website that is hard to use.
The gender gap is especially stubborn.
Globally, around 70 percent of men use the
internet, compared with about 65 percent
of women. That five-point gap represents
hundreds of millions of people. Behind
every percentage point is a person who
cannot reach the same information,
services, and opportunities as everyone
else.
Why does this matter? The internet is no
longer a luxury channel. It is where jobs
are posted, where education happens, where
governments deliver services, and where
small businesses find customers. When
people are offline, they miss more than
entertainment. They miss access to
opportunity, to a clinic appointment, to a
scholarship, or to a first customer. But
the evidence also shows that connection
alone is not enough. People need skills,
affordable devices, local language
content, and trust. Without those pieces,
a new connection often sits unused.
Digital inclusion is not a cable. It is a
system that has to work together.
What would close the gap? Three levers
matter most. First, infrastructure: extend
networks to rural and underserved areas,
and make sure electricity is reliable,
because a tower without power is just a
steel frame. Second, affordability: lower
the cost of devices and data, and design
subsidies that reach the people who need
them, not only the people who are easiest
to count. Third, skills and relevance:
teach digital literacy, support local
languages, and build services people
actually need. No single lever is enough.
A cheap connection without a device is not
access. A device without skills is not
inclusion. And skills without affordable
data cannot last. Progress needs all three
at once, in the same places, at the same
time.
The internet reached five and a half
billion people faster than almost any
technology in history. But the next
billion will not be won by repeating the
same playbook. They will be won by solving
the hard problems: rural infrastructure,
affordability, devices, skills, and trust.
Each of those problems has a local face, a
particular village, a particular price, a
particular language. The global internet
is no longer only a story about
technology. It is a story about who gets
to participate, and who is still waiting
at the edge of the network. That is a
choice we are still making, every day.
